digest: Web summary (recipetineats.com, 4.91 (283)). Nagi Maehashi frames these as Australia's iconic ANZAC biscuit, tracing them to WWI-era soldiers' wives who devised a long-lasting biscuit for the months-long journey overseas, noting the originals were reportedly rock-hard. Her technical aim is a crisp edge with a slightly chewy center: golden syrup and butter are melted together, baking soda is stirred in (causing a fizzing reaction) before mixing into the dry ingredients, and bake time is the main lever - 15 minutes for crisp, 12 for chewier. She pre-empts sweetness complaints in her own recipe note, warning that cutting sugar sacrifices crispness. What readers report: RecipeTin doesn't display vote counts on individual comments, so weight can't be gauged that way. Several readers echo the sweetness concern (one suggests halving sugar to 1/2 cup) and others report crumbly dough or finished biscuits; the fix repeated back by commenters is Nagi's own guidance - add butter if too dry, add flour if too wet. One reader questions whether the published nutrition figures (74 cal/biscuit) are correct. A technique tip from one baker: don't flatten the dough until halfway through baking and shorten the time to avoid burnt undersides. Another successfully substituted wholegrain oats and shredded coconut for the specified rolled oats and desiccated coconut, baking 14 minutes. One commenter objects to the biscuits being called 'cookies.'

recipe: Baked Cod With Crunchy Lemon-Herb Topping
digest: Web summary (washingtonpost.com, no rating shown). Adapted from America's Test Kitchen's 2007 'Best of' collection and tested for the Post by Leigh Lambert, this is a fast, technique-driven approach to a delicate white fish: a garlic-lemon mayonnaise is brushed onto the cod first, both to season it and to act as glue for a coarse buttery-cracker-and-herb crumb topping, which bakes at high heat (450 degrees F) for just 15 minutes so the crumbs turn golden and crunchy while the fish stays moist underneath. The recipe's own technical note flags that the crackers must be crushed to pea-sized crumbs rather than fine ones, or they won't crisp properly in the oven. What readers report: this page shows no reader comments or reviews - the rating widget reads 'Be the first to rate' and the review count is zero, so there is no reader feedback, corrections, or substitution data to distil. Any assessment of how the recipe performs in practice would have to come from another source.

Web summary (foodandwine.com, 5.0 (4)). Written by Christian Delouvrier, this is a weeknight shortcut: rather than true barbecue, a pork loin is seared then oven-roasted at 375 degrees F, brushed midway with a ketchup-based sauce (honey, Dijon, soy sauce, red wine vinegar) that's reduced afterward into a caramelized glaze served alongside. The site's own FAQ addresses two technical points: searing before roasting for color and flavor, and preventing dryness by resting at least 10 minutes and pulling the roast around 140 degrees F to account for carryover cooking rather than waiting for the USDA's 145 degrees F. What readers report: only four reviews, none showing helpfulness or vote counts beyond a zero-reply tally, so weighting can't be inferred from votes. The most substantive note comes from a reader who scaled the recipe to a 9-pound boneless loin, cut and seared it in two batches, roasted it on a sheet pan, and had to tent it with foil for the last 30 minutes because the sauce began to burn - a caution for anyone scaling up or extending roasting time. Two other reviewers turned the sauce into a marinade instead of a basting glaze - one marinating 5 hours before searing/roasting, another marinating and then finishing on the grill. The fourth review is brief praise with no detail.

Web summary (epicurious.com / Bon Appetit, 4.0 (192); 163 notes). The headnote is actually a reader's own request, printed as the framing: Marganne Hoffman of Lebanon, PA recalls a cheddar-crusted broccoli soup from Russell's restaurant near her college and asked Bon Appetit to recreate it, so the recipe reconstructs a remembered restaurant dish finished under a broiler with a cheddar crust rather than cheese stirred into the pot. What readers report: the most cited correction comes from a longtime home cook and blogger (frugal_hausfrau) who says that after years making it and reading the reviews, she identified an actual flaw in the recipe causing texture problems, and wrote up techniques and a fix on her blog; two later commenters (esleigh, oldlymefoodie) explicitly credit her link for showing them the beurre manie thickening step and for troubleshooting. A detailed technique note (13 years ago) recommends sweating and pureeing the onions and broccoli stems to thicken and intensify flavor instead of relying on the roux alone, swapping the tarragon for thyme, substituting half-and-half for cream, and adding significantly more salt (about 2.5 tsp) and white pepper - though another commenter strongly disputes dropping the tarragon, calling it essential. Multiple reviewers independently note the soup needs extra salt, and one calls the finished soup too thin. A common practical substitution: stirring the cheese directly into the soup rather than broiling a crust on top, especially for meal prep. Reaction counts on individual comments are low, mostly 0-3.

Web summary (bonappetit.com, 4.1 (1559)). Sue Li and Chris Morocco's headnote frames this as a back-to-basics classic Caesar, built on raw egg yolks and anchovies to make a dressing that coats without weighing the leaves down, with a callout that shaved (not grated) Parmesan avoids muting the dressing under clumped cheese. What readers report: the most substantive note (Ale Jacchia, 1 reaction) is a historical correction — inventor Caesar Cardini's original dressing used both anchovies and Worcestershire, not one or the other — and the commenter adds both, plus chills washed romaine wrapped in a towel for extra crispness. Two readers (Kenneth; Eric) report the finished dressing runs thin and light-bodied, with Eric blaming the 1/2 cup vegetable oil specifically and finding most quantities besides anchovies too skimpy. Several push back on the vegetable oil itself, preferring all olive oil (QSKE, 1 reaction) or substitutes like corn oil (Andy P) or avocado oil (Jimbo Slice, 1 reaction). A veteran maker (Sequitur, 2 reactions, ~40 batches) swaps an emulsifier for hand-whisking and pre-marinates the bread cubes in oil and smashed garlic before baking, though a reply questions whether that emulsifier method turns the olive oil bitter. Others substitute mayonnaise for the yolk-and-oil emulsion (DARI, 1 reaction) or use anchovy paste with pre-soaked garlic (Madagascar).

Web summary (foodandwine.com, 4.4 (8)). Jason Travi's headnote frames this as a fast, five-ingredient formula — blanch, then saute in garlic- and chile-infused olive oil, finished with a splash of the reserved cooking water for a light glaze — pitched as adaptable to other mild vegetables like cauliflower or green beans. What readers report: the dominant, repeated fix is that the recipe's 1-3 minute blanch overcooks the broccolini into mush; several independent commenters (MustardPecan1894; StrivingMango9305; AmbitiousRefrigerator8531; CapableOven3352) cut the blanch to about 1 minute or swap it for a brief steam, and the page's flagged 'most helpful positive review' (EffervescentStrawberry2990) skips blanching entirely, sauteing the broccolini directly in the garlic-chile oil, then covering and steaming with a little water. One commenter (JovialFish8040) accidentally omitted the reserved cooking water step and found the dish better for it — less mushy — though they preferred it served hot rather than at the room temperature the recipe suggests. Another (dustylnguyen) recommends an ice bath after blanching to stop the cooking and preserve color when it won't be eaten right away. No numeric helpfulness votes are shown beyond the 'most helpful' label; only small reply counts (0-1) appear on the reviews.

Web summary (epicurious.com, 4.4 (34)). In the visible portion of her headnote, Dorie Greenspan presents these cheese choux puffs as a French classic she's often asked to make by French friends and one of her most-requested recipes; most of her technical framing sits behind Epicurious's paywall. What readers report: the clearest correction is that the recipe's 5 eggs is too many, making the dough too runny and the baked puffs flat unless piped very small (a 14-year-old comment, echoed independently by BavarianCook, who used one fewer egg and less cheese with good results). A related fix, credited to another reviewer, is to bake until deep golden-brown, since underbaked puffs collapse; agasque adds that beating the dough longer than instructed also helps it hold its shape. One reader (Pariscafe) reports a full failure — flat, flavorless discs — and blames the recipe's dough-consistency description ('dry' dough) as too vague to gauge. Technique notes include sifting the flour for smoother dough (SZEIGLER) and mixing by hand rather than machine for better rise (Smaggy66), though abedvm used a stand mixer successfully. Multiple readers confirm both dough and baked puffs freeze well, including baking straight from frozen two months later (christopherbromsey), but leftovers should not go in the microwave, which turns them soft and limp (agasque). No vote or helpfulness counts are shown on the page.

Web summary (foodandwine.com, 5.0 (5)). Barbara Lynch's headnote positions this as a beginner-friendly formula for grilling whole fish: stuff gutted branzino with lemon slices and herbs, oil and season the skin, and leave it undisturbed on the grill so it releases naturally and stays crisp, flipping only once. A Test Kitchen sidebar adds that most branzino sold today is farm-raised due to overfishing concerns and suggests having the fishmonger pre-scale and gut the fish. What readers report: there are no corrections or errors flagged — all seven reviews are positive and the recipe holds a perfect 5.0 rating. The most substantive input is a stovetop adaptation from an apartment-dwelling reader (Pamela19123), who cooks it in a cast-iron grill pan and warns it produces significant smoke requiring ventilation, and notes a finishing squeeze of lemon makes a real difference. Another reader (Mike Affinito, on his fifth batch of the summer) recommends real lump charcoal over other grill fuels for the best flavor, otherwise following the recipe as written. One commenter (Richard) asks what comparable whole fish is available in North America/Canada, since branzino can be hard to source, but the question goes unanswered on the page. No vote or helpfulness counts are shown, only reply counts, all at zero.

Web summary (liquor.com, 4.0 (627), 16 reviews). Liquor.com's unsigned staff framing traces the Mai Tai's contested origin between Trader Vic Bergeron and Don the Beachcomber in the 1930s-40s, notes its slide into sugary mixer-drink territory before the Tiki revival restored a rum-forward style, and frames this build around blending a white rum base with a dark rum float, dry (not blue) orange curacao, almond-true orgeat and fresh lime. What readers report: several commenters dispute the recipe's authenticity rather than just tweaking it -- one says true Mai Tais don't use white rum at all, another calls it 'terrible,' arguing that color terms (white/dark) say nothing about flavor and that the original Trader Vic drink uses an aged Jamaican rum plus a Martinique rum, all shaken together with no floater. A third makes the same color-terminology point, recommending aged Jamaican rum with agricole instead. Technique note: one reader tried floating Morgan's Spiced as the dark rum and found it wasn't dense/dark enough to actually float, implying the float needs a heavier rum like Smith & Cross Navy Strength (used successfully by another commenter, who also upped the orgeat to 3/4 oz). Common substitution questions, left unanswered by the author: Triple Sec or Cointreau in place of curacao, Malibu for the white rum, and what orgeat even is. No vote or helpfulness counts are shown on any comment.

Web summary (simplyrecipes.com, 5.0 (4) shown, but 0 written reviews). Mark Beahm, a former professional baker who says he prefers rustic home desserts to finicky, decoration-heavy ones, introduces migliaccio, a ricotta-and-semolina cake from Campania traditionally eaten at Carnevale, describing its texture as landing between a plain cake and a cheesecake. He explains the technique goal: cooking semolina into a milk porridge on the stove before folding in cooled eggs and ricotta gives richness and creaminess without needing a water bath or extra dairy, and the same pan is used throughout to save on dishes. He flavors it with lemon zest, vanilla and a pinch of cinnamon (rather than the traditional Fiori di Sicilia extract), and recommends chilling it overnight so the flavors meld, though it can also be eaten warm and pudding-like straight from the oven. What readers report: none -- despite a 5.0 rating shown from 4 ratings at the top of the page, the reviews section itself reads 'Be the first to review!', meaning no written comments, corrections, or substitutions have actually been posted.

Web summary (latimes.com, no rating or review count shown). This is a 2014 Los Angeles Times Test Kitchen feature presenting Nancy Silverton's professional bakery method for basic focaccia dough, built around a slow pre-ferment: a wallpaper-paste-consistency sponge made with a tiny amount of cake yeast, water and bread flour, left at 68-70F for 12 to 24 hours before being mixed into the final dough. The final dough adds rye flour, more yeast, olive oil and salt, is mixed in a stand mixer to a specific pull-away-from-the-bowl consistency, and undergoes a bulk rise, a fold, a second rise, then division into two 18-ounce rounds pressed into oiled cake pans -- all specified by weight in ounces on a digital scale, reflecting Silverton's bakery-trained precision. The piece is framed as one installment of a Nancy Silverton recipe series the paper's Test Kitchen ran, inviting readers to submit photos of their results for the food blog. What readers report: this page as captured shows no comment or review section at all -- there is no reader feedback to summarize, positive or corrective.

Web summary (thespruceeats.com, 3.9 (38), 4 reviews). Molly Watson's crisp for The Spruce Eats (tested by Joan Velush) swaps in Asian pears -- or substitutes like Anjou or Bosc -- under a whole-wheat-pastry-flour crumble topping, seasoning the fruit with garam masala, cardamom, ginger and cloves instead of the usual cinnamon for what she frames as a lighter, juicier take on a standard fruit crisp; she notes all-purpose flour or rolled oats can stand in for the whole wheat pastry flour, and cinnamon can replace the spice blend if preferred. The tester's note, quoted on the page, warns that because Asian pears are so juicy, the baked dish may pool more liquid at the bottom than a typical crisp. What readers report: there is essentially no substantive feedback. Of the four reviews, none contains a correction, technique fix, or substitution -- two are brief praise ('amazing,' a church-choir crowd 'loved it'), and two are site-usability complaints unrelated to the recipe itself (unable to save or print the page, and no photos shown). No vote or helpfulness counts appear on any comment.

Web summary (williams-sonoma.com, 3.0 (2)). The recipe is credited to Thomas Keller of The French Laundry; the framing treats rösti as a basic template — grated, salted, squeezed-dry potatoes pressed and browned in clarified butter, then finished in a 350°F oven — that a cook can embellish with bacon, minced onion or other add-ins. What readers report: only two reviews exist, both mixed-to-critical. One reviewer (2 helpful votes vs. 10 unhelpful) calls the dish 'completely inedible' because of the salt: 1 Tbs. kosher salt for 3 medium potatoes was excessive in her and her husband's judgment, and she notes they scaled the recipe up proportionally rather than deviating from its ratio, so this reads as a genuine complaint about the recipe's salt level rather than a cook's error. She adds the effort of grating is as expected and not itself a problem. The other reviewer (1 helpful vote, 0 unhelpful) rated it 5 stars but flagged it as a lot of work for a small yield, noting it can be made ahead and reheated. No technique fixes or substitutions are offered beyond these two points.

Web summary (bonappetit.com, 4.1 (342)). Carla Lalli Music's 2014 recipe rubs a whole chicken with a fennel-seed and chile-flake spice paste, stuffs it with lemon, garlic and herbs, and slow-roasts it at 300°F on a bed of Yukon Golds for about 3 hours to produce shreddable, tender meat rather than the texture of a faster high-heat roast. What readers report (25 notes): the most substantive fix is on timing — several cooks, including one who hit 180°F (15 degrees past done) after only 1.5 hours and another whose 5-lb. bird was already dry at 3 hours in a calibrated oven, warn the stated time is a ceiling, not a guarantee, and the bird should be temped well before the 3-hour mark. Multiple commenters independently confirm the oven must not be run on convection, which several blame for dry results. One clears up a point of confusion in the recipe: the 'basting liquid' isn't anything added — it's the chicken's own rendered fat, so a lid works as well as basting. A typo is flagged ('pepper flakes,' not 'paper flakes'). Reader-tested substitutions that hold up: dried herbs (including herbes de Provence) at half the fresh quantity work well; rubbing paste under the breast skin as well as over it is called an improvement; one suggests trussing with a needle rather than string for better results.

Web summary (bonappetit.com, 4.0 (48)). Melissa Hamilton and Christopher Hirsheimer's 2010 recipe uses a vegetable peeler to turn raw asparagus spears into thin ribbons, dressed with a Parmesan-lemon vinaigrette and topped with more shaved Parmesan; the framing presents the peeling technique as a general trick for transforming raw vegetable texture, applicable to carrots and zucchini as well as asparagus, not just a one-off preparation. What readers report: nothing — the page shows zero recipe notes, with the site's own placeholder reading 'There aren't any recipe notes yet. Be the first to start the conversation!' So there are no corrections, technique fixes, or substitutions to distill from this page; the only reader signal at all is the aggregate 4.0 star rating from 48 ratings, with no accompanying written feedback.

Web summary (thespruceeats.com, 4.0 (141), 13 Reviews). Diana Rattray's recipe (tested by Carrie Parente, updated Aug. 2025) sears bone-in pork chops, then braises them low and covered in a pan sauce of chicken broth, Dijon, brown sugar, cider vinegar and Worcestershire with softened onion and garlic, aiming for tender chops with minimal fuss. What readers report: the most developed correction (with 4 replies) comes from a reviewer who followed the recipe exactly and got dry meat — she diagnoses the cause as the instructed medium heat, which suits the onions but is too low to properly sear the pork, and recommends searing the chops in a hot pan first, removing them, then building the onion mixture afterward. This matches two separate short complaints that the meat came out tough or chewy despite following the Dijon method, and a blunter review calling these 'the worst pork cooking instructions,' though allowing the sauce has potential. A step-numbering question ('how did seared pork chops become raw again' in Step 7) points to a possible discontinuity in the written steps. Common substitutions: one cook cut brown sugar from 3 Tbs. to 1 Tbs. for a low-sugar version, doubled the sauce, and added a small sliced apple, calling the Worcestershire the key flavor addition; another asked, unanswered, about swapping rice wine vinegar for cider vinegar; others added sherry, extra Worcestershire, and suggested a touch of anchovy for depth.

recipe: Lemony Asparagus Pasta (Spaghetti al Limone With Asparagus)
digest: Web summary (bonappetit.com, 4.6 (126), 44 notes). Evan Funke's asparagus pasta (first printed 2020), framed by BA editors as a quick, craftsmanship-forward dish where thinly sliced asparagus and an emulsified Parmesan-lemon-olive oil sauce, finished with starchy pasta water, are meant to complement the noodles rather than overwhelm them. What readers report: the clearest recurring correction is that the recipe under-specifies lemon quantity — it calls for '2 lemons' rather than a juice volume, and because lemon size and juiciness vary widely, multiple independent readers report batches that turned out too sour or overpoweringly lemony; one explicitly asks the site to give a juice measurement instead, and another cautions to add zest and juice gradually to avoid an overpowering result. A second cluster says the dish runs oily as written and suggests cutting back the oil, with one reviewer also calling the vegetable-to-pasta ratio off and the result bland. A separate commenter flags a mismatch between the written recipe and the site's test-kitchen video, which shows heavy cream, butter and no asparagus at all. Reader-tested tweaks that held up: cooking the asparagus separately for about 2 minutes just before the pasta finishes to preserve its color, and mixing everything directly in the pasta pot rather than transferring to a skillet; pressing rather than smashing the garlic; and dialing back the red pepper flakes to taste.
